title: The Leadership Theater: Everyone’s a Leader, Nobody’s in Charge
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Jain opens with an encounter at a school career fair in which a polished executive with a six-word title cannot say what he is responsible for, and uses it to argue that corporate leadership has become performance. In Act I he says inflated titles and proximity to power create leadership without ownership, so decisions stall behind buzzwords and committees. In Act II he argues that busyness is the modern badge of leadership, and that leaders themselves direct the play by scheduling meetings and rewarding visibility over value. He names the costs as decision paralysis, complexity theater, empty grind, eroded trust and suffocated creativity, drawing on his own two decades in tech. In Act III he claims AI is exposing what was only performance, since slides, summaries and polished emails can now be generated instantly. What remains is judgment, courage, clarity and accountability, and the remedy is behavioral unlearning rather than new tools.
points: Argues that titles grant permission, not power, and that real authority comes from making decisions and being accountable when things go wrong.
Claims buzzword-heavy leadership is a safety strategy, because sounding important is less risky than making a decision that creates friction.
Diagnoses busyness as avoidance: while you are in a meeting or aligning, you do not have to decide or be accountable.
Says leaders themselves cause the erosion of trust, because teams see through performance faster than leaders realize and quietly disengage.
Predicts AI will strip away the props of leadership, leaving judgment, courage, clarity and accountability, and asks leaders to unlearn performance habits.
quotes: As a corporate society, we’ve quietly entered an era of leadership where everyone’s a leader, yet nobody’s in charge.
We’ve made leadership “sound sophisticated” when it should be simple: See the problem Make a decision Take responsibility That’s it.

We think the title gives us authority. But titles only grant permission, not power. Real authority doesn’t come from what’s printed on an org chart. It comes from making decisions where they matter, owning, and being accountable when things go wrong.
But here’s the uncomfortable truth: WE as leaders are the ones directing this play.

They know when a meeting is theater: when words like “momentum” or “alignment” are covering the lack of courage to make a decision. At first, they may play along. But after a while, I guarantee you, they will stop believing the story.

In fact, our obsession with visibility often robs us of the one thing that makes leadership possible - perspective. When every minute is filled with meetings, updates, and check-ins, we have no time left to think.
What can be automated was probably never the essence of leadership to begin with.
